And Rukn al-Din accepted the command,
and on one of the nights he came down, he with his children and his household,
and he was well received by the King of Kings,
and he was sent to the city of Qazwin with honor.
Indeed, those three hundred horsemen the Mongols killed secretly,
and they gained control moreover over the fortress from which Rukn al-Din had come down,
the one named Maymun-Diz,
and they destroyed it.
Likewise, also the strong fortress called Alamut,
and the fortress called Gerdkuh, which was situated in the heart of heaven,
and fifty other fortresses around it, the Tatars took, and destroyed, and demolished,
and they killed all those who were in them.
And in these blessed campaigns,
God had mercy on all the kings of the Arabs and of the Christians, who had been in trembling and shaking from the dread of the Ismailites,
these dagger-bearers and shedders of innocent blood.
Then Rukn al-Din, when he saw that Hulagu's mercies were revealed toward him, said to him openly:
"These days in which I now live,
You in Your grace have added to me.
Henceforth, I beg that you grant me permission to spend them pleasantly."
And he commanded the treasurers that an ample supply of gold and silver be given to him.
And when he took it,
he began to eat and to drink and to revel.
And he fell in love with one of the Mongol maidens,
and Hulagu commanded, and she was given to him as a wife.
And one day, while he was drinking wine,
he said to a certain citharode,
and he sang this verse: "As to a physician, to you, I, your sick one, have come,
O King of Kings; and to acquire life, to meet you I have come.
To pluck the healthy fruits of your seed I have come;
otherwise, for what merchandise, pray, to your land have I come?"
in Persian. And when Hulagu heard these things,
his words pleased him greatly,
and he was regarded with favor in his eyes.
